summary: A compact cryogenic noise source based on a chromium on-chip attenuator heated with nanowatt-level DC power enables in situ calibration of microwave drive-line attenuation and amplifier noise by comparing Johnson–Nyquist noise generated via Joule and RF heating. The method determines input-line attenuation to ±0.5 dB over 4–8 GHz with millisecond thermal response times and negligible cryostat perturbation, yielding 23.6 ± 2.8 photons of added noise and 70.2 ± 0.5 dB gain for a HEMT-based readout chain.
motivation: Accurate in situ characterization of drive-line attenuation and amplifier gain/noise temperature is essential for superconducting-qubit experiments, but existing cryogenic calibration methods either work only over narrow frequency bands, require complex modifications to wiring, or suffer from slow thermal response times on the order of minutes.
method: A 60 nm chromium attenuator in T-network configuration on sapphire is resistively heated via a four-probe bias-tee connection at the mixing chamber and thermally isolated from the rest of the circuit via superconducting niobium leads; attenuation is extracted by least-squares fitting of power spectral density measurements comparing Joule heating to RF heating across the signal power range −22.5 to −5 dBm where the on-chip attenuator dominates noise generation.
result: At 5.5 GHz, the method yields input-line attenuation of 76.3 ± 1 dB (validated against independent thermometer measurement), with thermal time constants of 0.25 ms (heating) and 1.57 ms (cooling), and characterizes the amplification chain as having 70.2 ± 0.5 dB gain and 23.6 ± 2.8 photons of system noise referenced to the noise-source output.
